sections.title: File Handling Basics — Conceptual Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
**Q1. What is the difference between `open()` with `close()` vs using `with` statement?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> Both open files, but the `with` statement (context manager) is vastly superior. With `close()`: if an exception occurs between `open()` and `close()`, the file is NEVER closed — causing file descriptor leaks. With the `with` statement, Python guarantees the file is closed via `__exit__()` method even if an exception occurs. In production, resource leaks from unclosed files cause: operating system file descriptor exhaustion (default limit ~1024 per process in Linux), data corruption (write buffers not flushed), and hard-to-debug issues. I never use manual `close()` in production code — always use `with open(...) as f:`. The `with` statement is essentially a try/finally block that Python handles automatically.

**Q2. What are all the file modes in Python and what does each do?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> There are 8 core modes: `'r'` (read-only, default), `'w'` (write, creates/overwrites), `'a'` (append, preserves content), `'x'` (exclusive create, fails if exists). Then combinations: `'r+'` (read+write without truncating), `'w+'` (write+read with truncating), `'a+'` (append+read). Add `'b'` for binary: `'rb'`, `'wb'`, `'ab'`. Critical gotchas: `'w'` mode SILENTLY deletes existing content — I've seen junior devs accidentally wipe databases. `'x'` mode is the safe create — prevents accidental overwrite. In production, I use `'r'` for config reading, `'w'` for report generation, `'a'` for logging, `'x'` when creating temp files that shouldn't overwrite existing.

**Q3. What does the encoding parameter do and why is UTF-8 the standard?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> The `encoding` parameter tells Python how to convert bytes (what's stored on disk) to characters (what you see in Python strings). If you open a UTF-8 file with ASCII encoding, you get `UnicodeDecodeError` for any non-ASCII character. UTF-8 is the web standard — it can represent every Unicode character while being backward compatible with ASCII. Without specifying encoding, Python uses the system default (which varies — UTF-8 on Linux/Mac, often cp1252 on Windows). I ALWAYS explicitly specify `encoding='utf-8'` in production code for portability. Real bug I fixed: an application worked on developer Mac but crashed on Windows server because of different default encodings.

**Q4. What is the difference between text mode and binary mode?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> Text mode (`'r'`, `'w'`): Python automatically handles encoding/decoding and newline translation (`\n` on Unix, `\r\n` on Windows). You work with `str` objects. Binary mode (`'rb'`, `'wb'`): no encoding/decoding, no newline translation. You work with `bytes` objects. Use text mode for: `.txt`, `.csv`, `.json`, `.log`, `.html`, `.py` — any human-readable file. Use binary mode for: images (`.jpg`, `.png`), videos, PDFs, `.zip`, `.xlsx`, executables, pickled Python objects. Critical: opening an image in text mode corrupts it because Python tries to decode bytes as text. In web development, always serve static files in binary mode.

**Q5. What happens to the write buffer when a file is closed?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> Python (and the OS) use **write buffers** for performance — data isn't written to disk immediately but accumulated in memory first. When you call `close()` (or exit the `with` block), Python **flushes** the buffer — forces all buffered data to disk. If your program crashes before closing, buffered data is LOST. Solutions: (1) Use `with` statement — always flushes on exit. (2) Call `f.flush()` explicitly after critical writes. (3) Open with `buffering=0` (unbuffered, only for binary mode). In logging systems, I use `flush=True` or configure the handler to flush immediately for critical logs — I've seen server crashes where last 100 log lines were lost because the buffer wasn't flushed.

**Q6. Can you open multiple files simultaneously in a single `with` statement?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> Yes! Python supports multiple context managers in one `with` statement:
>
> ```python
> # Python 3.10+
> with (open("input.txt") as fin,
>       open("output.txt", "w") as fout,
>       open("log.txt", "a") as flog):
>     data = fin.read()
>     fout.write(data.upper())
>     flog.write("Processing complete\n")
>
> # Works in all Python 3 versions:
> with open("input.txt") as fin, open("output.txt", "w") as fout:
>     fout.write(fin.read())
> ```
>
> I use this pattern regularly for ETL pipelines — reading from source, writing to destination, logging to log file, all in one clean block. All files are guaranteed to close even if an exception occurs mid-processing.

**Q7. What is `f.seek()` and `f.tell()` used for?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `f.tell()` returns the current **byte position** of the file pointer. `f.seek(offset, whence)` moves the pointer. `whence=0` (default) — from beginning, `whence=1` — from current position, `whence=2` — from end. Classic uses: (1) Read file, seek back to beginning to read again: `f.seek(0)`. (2) Find file size: `f.seek(0,2); size = f.tell()`. (3) Read last N bytes: `f.seek(-100, 2); last_100 = f.read()`. (4) Resume incomplete downloads. (5) Random access in binary files (like database files). I used `seek()` to implement a "tail -f" log monitoring tool — reading only new content added to a log file since last check.

sections.body:
**S1. Your application opens thousands of files in a loop. After some time, you get "Too many open files" error. What's the cause and fix?**

> **Answer:**
>
> ```python
> import os
> import resource  # Unix only
>
> # ❌ BAD — files opened but never closed properly
> def process_files_bad(file_paths):
>     file_handles = []
>     for path in file_paths:
>         f = open(path, 'r')  # Opens file
>         file_handles.append(f)
>         # If exception here, files never closed!
>         content = f.read()
>         process(content)
>     # Even if we close at end, exception = leak
>     for f in file_handles:
>         f.close()
>
> # ✅ GOOD — with statement guarantees closing
> def process_files_good(file_paths):
>     results = []
>     for path in file_paths:
>         try:
>             with open(path, 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f:  # auto-closed!
>                 content = f.read()
>                 results.append(process_content(content))
>         except FileNotFoundError:
>             print(f"Skipping missing file: {path}")
>         except PermissionError:
>             print(f"Skipping inaccessible file: {path}")
>     return results
>
> # Check current file descriptor limits
> def check_fd_limits():
>     import subprocess
>     # Show current open file descriptors
>     pid = os.getpid()
>     try:
>         result = subprocess.run(
>             ['lsof', '-p', str(pid), '-n'],
>             capture_output=True, text=True
>         )
>         fd_count = len(result.stdout.strip().split('\n'))
>         print(f"Open file descriptors: {fd_count}")
>     except:
>         pass
>
>     # Check system limits
>     try:
>         soft, hard = resource.getrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_NOFILE)
>         print(f"Soft limit: {soft}, Hard limit: {hard}")
>     except:
>         pass
>
> def process_content(content):
>     return len(content)  # simplified
>
> # Test with actual files
> test_files = ["example.txt"]
> results = process_files_good(test_files)
> print(f"Processed {len(results)} files")
> ```

**S2. You need to process a 10GB log file. How do you read it without running out of memory?**

> **Answer:**
>
> ```python
> import os
>
> # ❌ BAD — loads ENTIRE file into memory at once!
> def process_large_file_bad(filepath):
>     with open(filepath, 'r') as f:
>         content = f.read()      # 10GB in RAM = MemoryError!
>         lines   = content.split('\n')  # another 10GB!
>         for line in lines:
>             process_line(line)
>
> # ✅ GOOD — Process line by line (constant memory usage!)
> def process_large_file_streaming(filepath):
>     """
>     Memory usage: constant ~8KB (one line at a time)
>     regardless of file size — works for 10GB, 100GB, 1TB
>     """
>     stats = {"total_lines": 0, "error_lines": 0, "processed": 0}
>
>     with open(filepath, 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f:
>         for line in f:          # Python reads one line at a time!
>             line = line.strip()
>             if not line:
>                 continue
>
>             stats["total_lines"] += 1
>             try:
>                 process_line(line)
>                 stats["processed"] += 1
>             except Exception:
>                 stats["error_lines"] += 1
>
>     return stats
>
> # ✅ EVEN BETTER — chunked reading for binary/non-line files
> def process_in_chunks(filepath, chunk_size=8192):
>     """Read in fixed-size chunks — for binary files"""
>     total_bytes = 0
>     with open(filepath, 'rb') as f:
>         while True:
>             chunk = f.read(chunk_size)  # Read 8KB at a time
>             if not chunk:
>                 break                   # End of file
>             total_bytes += len(chunk)
>             process_chunk(chunk)
>     return total_bytes
>
> # ✅ BEST — generator for lazy evaluation
> def file_line_generator(filepath, encoding='utf-8'):
>     """Generator — yields one line at a time"""
>     with open(filepath, 'r', encoding=encoding) as f:
>         for line_num, line in enumerate(f, 1):
>             yield line_num, line.rstrip('\n')
>
> def process_line(line): pass
> def process_chunk(chunk): pass
>
> # Create a sample file to test
> with open("large_sample.txt", "w") as f:
>     for i in range(1000):
>         f.write(f"2024-01-15 {i:02d}:00:00 INFO Processing record {i}\n")
>
> # Use the generator
> for line_num, line in file_line_generator("large_sample.txt"):
>     if "ERROR" in line:
>         print(f"Line {line_num}: {line}")
>
> stats = process_large_file_streaming("large_sample.txt")
> print(f"Stats: {stats}")
> os.remove("large_sample.txt")
> ```

**S3. You need to safely write to a file — if writing fails halfway, the original file should remain intact. How?**

> **Answer:**
>
> ```python
> import os
> import tempfile
> import shutil
>
> def atomic_write(filepath, content, encoding='utf-8'):
>     """
>     Atomic file write — either fully succeeds or original unchanged.
>     Pattern: write to temp file → rename (atomic on most OS).
>     Used in: database systems, config files, any critical data.
>     """
>     # Get directory of target file
>     dir_path = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(filepath))
>
>     # Create temp file in SAME directory (same filesystem for atomic rename)
>     fd, temp_path = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=dir_path, suffix='.tmp')
>
>     try:
>         # Write to temp file
>         with os.fdopen(fd, 'w', encoding=encoding) as temp_file:
>             temp_file.write(content)
>             temp_file.flush()
>             os.fsync(temp_file.fileno())  # Force write to physical disk
>
>         # Atomic rename: temp → target
>         # On Unix: rename() is atomic
>         # On Windows: replace() is atomic
>         if os.name == 'nt':  # Windows
>             os.replace(temp_path, filepath)
>         else:  # Unix/Linux/Mac
>             os.rename(temp_path, filepath)
>
>         print(f"✅ Successfully wrote to {filepath}")
>         return True
>
>     except Exception as e:
>         # Cleanup temp file on failure
>         try:
>             os.unlink(temp_path)
>         except OSError:
>             pass
>         print(f"❌ Write failed: {e}")
>         return False
>
> # Test it
> # First write
> atomic_write("config.json", '{"version": 1, "debug": false}')
>
> # Simulate failure mid-write (original preserved)
> original_content = open("config.json").read() if os.path.exists("config.json") else ""
>
> def simulate_write_failure():
>     dir_path = "."
>     fd, temp_path = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=dir_path, suffix='.tmp')
>     try:
>         with os.fdopen(fd, 'w') as f:
>             f.write("PARTIAL CORRUPT")
>             raise RuntimeError("Simulated disk full error!")  # Fails mid-write
>     except RuntimeError:
>         os.unlink(temp_path)  # cleanup
>         print("Write failed — original file untouched")
>
> simulate_write_failure()
> # Original config.json is still intact!
> if os.path.exists("config.json"):
>     print(f"Original safe: {open('config.json').read()}")
>     os.remove("config.json")
> ```

**S4. How do you handle file operations across different operating systems (Windows vs Linux)?**

> **Answer:**
>
> ```python
> import os
> import sys
> from pathlib import Path
>
> class CrossPlatformFileHandler:
>     """
>     Handle file operations that work on Windows, Linux, and Mac.
>     Key differences:
>     - Path separators: \ (Windows) vs / (Unix)
>     - Line endings: \r\n (Windows) vs \n (Unix)
>     - Encoding defaults differ
>     - File permissions model differs
>     """
>
>     def __init__(self, base_dir):
>         # Use pathlib.Path — handles separators automatically!
>         self.base_dir = Path(base_dir)
>         self.base_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
>
>     def write_text_file(self, filename, content):
>         """
>         Cross-platform text write:
>         - Always specify encoding (don't rely on system default)
>         - Python handles \n → \r\n on Windows in text mode
>         """
>         filepath = self.base_dir / filename  # pathlib handles separators!
>
>         with open(filepath, 'w', encoding='utf-8',
>                   newline=None) as f:  # newline=None = universal newlines
>             f.write(content)
>
>         return filepath
>
>     def read_text_file(self, filename):
>         """Always read with explicit encoding"""
>         filepath = self.base_dir / filename
>
>         if not filepath.exists():
>             raise FileNotFoundError(f"File not found: {filepath}")
>
>         with open(filepath, 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f:
>             return f.read()
>
>     def safe_path(self, *parts):
>         """Build paths that work on any OS"""
>         return Path(*parts)   # handles all separator issues
>
>     def get_system_info(self):
>         return {
>             "os":          sys.platform,
>             "path_sep":    os.sep,         # \ on Windows, / on Unix
>             "line_ending": repr(os.linesep),
>             "encoding":    sys.getdefaultencoding(),
>             "cwd":         os.getcwd(),
>             "home":        str(Path.home()),
>             "temp_dir":    tempfile.gettempdir() if __import__('tempfile') else "N/A",
>         }
>
> import tempfile
>
> handler = CrossPlatformFileHandler("./test_crossplatform")
> handler.write_text_file("hello.txt", "Hello Cross-Platform World!\nLine 2\n")
> content = handler.read_text_file("hello.txt")
> print(f"Content: {repr(content)}")
>
> info = handler.get_system_info()
> for key, value in info.items():
>     print(f"  {key:<15}: {value}")
>
> # Cleanup
> shutil.rmtree("./test_crossplatform", ignore_errors=True)
> import shutil
> ```

**S5. You need to read a file that might not exist, or might be corrupted. How do you handle this gracefully?**

> **Answer:**
>
> ```python
> import os
> import json
>
> class RobustFileReader:
>     """
>     Graceful file reading with comprehensive error handling.
>     Real-world: config files, data files, user files.
>     """
>
>     def read_with_fallback(self, primary_path, fallback_path=None,
>                            default=None, encoding='utf-8'):
>         """Try primary → fallback → default"""
>         for path in [p for p in [primary_path, fallback_path] if p]:
>             try:
>                 with open(path, 'r', encoding=encoding) as f:
>                     content = f.read()
>                     if content.strip():  # not empty
>                         print(f"✅ Read from: {path}")
>                         return content, path
>                     else:
>                         print(f"⚠️  Empty file: {path}")
>             except FileNotFoundError:
>                 print(f"📁 Not found: {path}")
>             except PermissionError:
>                 print(f"🔒 No permission: {path}")
>             except UnicodeDecodeError:
>                 print(f"🔤 Encoding error: {path}")
>                 # Try with different encodings
>                 for enc in ['latin-1', 'cp1252', 'utf-16']:
>                     try:
>                         with open(path, 'r', encoding=enc) as f:
>                             return f.read(), path
>                     except (UnicodeDecodeError, LookupError):
>                         continue
>             except OSError as e:
>                 print(f"💥 OS Error {e.errno}: {e.strerror}: {path}")
>
>         print(f"⚠️  All paths failed — using default")
>         return default, None
>
>     def read_json_safely(self, path, default=None):
>         content, source = self.read_with_fallback(path, default="{}")
>         try:
>             return json.loads(content or "{}"), source
>         except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
>             print(f"⚠️  JSON parse error at {path}: {e}")
>             return default, None
>
> reader = RobustFileReader()
>
> # Test various scenarios
> with open("good_file.txt", "w", encoding='utf-8') as f:
>     f.write("Good content here")
>
> content, source = reader.read_with_fallback(
>     "missing.txt",
>     "good_file.txt",
>     default="DEFAULT CONTENT"
> )
> print(f"Content: {content[:20]}, Source: {source}\n")
>
> content, source = reader.read_with_fallback(
>     "totally_missing.txt",
>     "also_missing.txt",
>     default="DEFAULT CONTENT"
> )
> print(f"Content: {content}, Source: {source}")
>
> os.remove("good_file.txt")
> ```

**S6. How do you implement a simple file-based lock to prevent multiple processes from writing simultaneously?**

> **Answer:**
>
> ```python
> import os
> import time
> import errno
>
> class FileLock:
>     """
>     Simple file-based lock for cross-process synchronization.
>     Used when multiple processes/scripts must not write to same file.
>     Real world: cron jobs, multiprocessing, distributed systems.
>     """
>     def __init__(self, lock_file, timeout=10, retry_delay=0.1):
>         self.lock_file   = lock_file
>         self.timeout     = timeout
>         self.retry_delay = retry_delay
>         self.locked      = False
>
>     def acquire(self):
>         """Try to acquire the lock"""
>         start_time = time.time()
>
>         while True:
>             try:
>                 # O_CREAT | O_EXCL = create file, fail if exists (ATOMIC!)
>                 fd = os.open(self.lock_file,
>                              os.O_CREAT | os.O_EXCL | os.O_WRONLY)
>                 # Write PID for debugging
>                 os.write(fd, str(os.getpid()).encode())
>                 os.close(fd)
>                 self.locked = True
>                 return True
>
>             except OSError as e:
>                 if e.errno != errno.EEXIST:
>                     raise  # Unexpected error
>
>                 # Lock exists — check if it's stale
>                 if self._is_stale_lock():
>                     self._remove_lock()
>                     continue
>
>                 # Check timeout
>                 if time.time() - start_time > self.timeout:
>                     return False  # Timeout!
>
>                 time.sleep(self.retry_delay)
>
>     def release(self):
>         """Release the lock"""
>         if self.locked:
>             try:
>                 os.unlink(self.lock_file)
>                 self.locked = False
>             except OSError:
>                 pass
>
>     def _is_stale_lock(self):
>         """Check if lock file is stale (process died)"""
>         try:
>             with open(self.lock_file, 'r') as f:
>                 pid = int(f.read().strip())
>             # Check if process still running
>             os.kill(pid, 0)  # Signal 0 = just check
>             return False  # Process alive, lock valid
>         except (ProcessLookupError, PermissionError):
>             return True   # Process dead, stale lock
>         except (ValueError, IOError):
>             return True   # Corrupted lock file
>
>     def _remove_lock(self):
>         try:
>             os.unlink(self.lock_file)
>         except OSError:
>             pass
>
>     def __enter__(self):
>         if not self.acquire():
>             raise TimeoutError(f"Could not acquire lock: {self.lock_file}")
>         return self
>
>     def __exit__(self, *args):
>         self.release()
>
> # Usage:
> def write_critical_data(data):
>     with FileLock("data.lock", timeout=5) as lock:
>         with open("critical_data.txt", "a") as f:
>             f.write(f"{data}\n")
>             f.flush()
>     print(f"✅ Written: {data}")
>
> write_critical_data("Transaction: $1000 from A to B")
> write_critical_data("Transaction: $500 from C to D")
>
> if os.path.exists("critical_data.txt"):
>     print(open("critical_data.txt").read())
>     os.remove("critical_data.txt")
> ```

**S7. How do you monitor a file for changes in real-time (like `tail -f`)?**

> **Answer:**
>
> ```python
> import os
> import time
>
> class FileTailMonitor:
>     """
>     Monitor a file for new content in real-time.
>     Like Unix 'tail -f' command.
>     Real world: monitoring log files, watching for new records.
>     """
>     def __init__(self, filepath, encoding='utf-8'):
>         self.filepath  = filepath
>         self.encoding  = encoding
>         self.position  = 0   # track where we last read
>
>     def get_new_lines(self):
>         """Get only NEW lines added since last check"""
>         if not os.path.exists(self.filepath):
>             return []
>
>         current_size = os.path.getsize(self.filepath)
>
>         # File truncated (log rotation) — reset position
>         if current_size < self.position:
>             print(f"⚠️  File truncated — resetting position")
>             self.position = 0
>
>         # No new content
>         if current_size == self.position:
>             return []
>
>         # Read only NEW content
>         with open(self.filepath, 'r', encoding=self.encoding) as f:
>             f.seek(self.position)      # Jump to where we left off
>             new_content = f.read()     # Read only new content
>             self.position = f.tell()   # Update position
>
>         return [line for line in new_content.split('\n') if line.strip()]
>
>     def tail(self, callback, poll_interval=0.5, max_iterations=None):
>         """Continuously monitor file, calling callback for new lines"""
>         # Start from end of existing file
>         if os.path.exists(self.filepath):
>             self.position = os.path.getsize(self.filepath)
>
>         iteration = 0
>         print(f"👀 Monitoring {self.filepath}...")
>
>         while True:
>             new_lines = self.get_new_lines()
>             for line in new_lines:
>                 callback(line)
>
>             time.sleep(poll_interval)
>             iteration += 1
>
>             if max_iterations and iteration >= max_iterations:
>                 break
>
> # Demo: write to file while monitoring
> log_file = "monitored.log"
>
> def on_new_line(line):
>     print(f"📥 New log: {line}")
>
> monitor = FileTailMonitor(log_file)
>
> # Simulate: write some log entries
> with open(log_file, "w") as f:
>     f.write("Existing log line 1\n")
>     f.write("Existing log line 2\n")
>
> # Get initial position (skip existing)
> monitor.position = os.path.getsize(log_file)
>
> # Add new content
> with open(log_file, "a") as f:
>     f.write("NEW: 2024-01-15 ERROR Something happened\n")
>     f.write("NEW: 2024-01-15 INFO  Recovery successful\n")
>
> # Check for new lines
> new_lines = monitor.get_new_lines()
> for line in new_lines:
>     on_new_line(line)
>
> os.remove(log_file)
> ```

sections.title: Reading & Writing Text Files — Conceptual Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
**Q1. What is the difference between `read()`, `readline()`, and `readlines()`?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `read()` reads the **entire file as one string** — loads everything into memory. `readline()` reads **one line at a time** — returns an empty string at EOF. `readlines()` reads **all lines into a list** — each element includes `\n`. For small files (< 100MB), any works. For large files, use `for line in f:` — it's Python's iterator protocol that reads one line at a time with minimal memory (constant ~buffer size memory vs file size memory). `readlines()` is useful when you need all lines in memory for random access or slicing. In production, I almost never use `read()` or `readlines()` for files that could be large — always use the iterator.

**Q2. Why does `write()` not add a newline automatically?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> By design — Python gives you control over exactly what's written. `write()` writes **exactly** what you pass. If it added `\n` automatically, you couldn't write partial lines or binary-like text. The trade-off: you must always remember to add `\n`. Common bugs: `f.write("Line 1"); f.write("Line 2")` — both on same line in file! Fix: either `f.write("Line 1\n")` or `print("Line 1", file=f)`. In production, I use `f.write(content + '\n')` for simple text, `print(..., file=f)` for formatted output, and `f.writelines([f"{line}\n" for line in lines])` for lists.

**Q3. What is the difference between `a` mode and `w` mode?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `'w'` (write) TRUNCATES the file to zero length first — any existing content is GONE. `'a'` (append) keeps existing content and writes new data at the END. Critical production concern: using `'w'` when you meant `'a'` is a data loss bug. Real scenario: log files must ALWAYS use `'a'` — using `'w'` would erase all previous logs on every server restart. Config files should use `'w'` when saving — you want to replace the entire config, not append to it. I was once part of a post-mortem where a developer used `'w'` on a customer database backup file — we lost the backup. Now I have a review checklist: always verify the mode for any file write operation.

**Q4. How does Python handle newlines across different operating systems?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> Windows uses `\r\n` (CRLF), Unix/Mac uses `\n` (LF). Python's text mode handles this automatically: on Windows, writing `\n` stores `\r\n` on disk; reading `\r\n` returns `\n`. This is called **universal newlines mode** (default). Problems arise with binary mode or the `newline` parameter. When sharing files between Windows and Unix, binary mode preserves exact bytes. The `newline=''` parameter disables translation (useful for CSV files — `csv` module handles its own newlines). In cross-platform applications, always use text mode for text files — Python handles the conversion. For critical binary data, use binary mode.

**Q5. What happens if you call `read()` twice on the same file object?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> The second `read()` returns an **empty string** because the file pointer is already at the end of file (EOF). The file pointer advances as you read. To read again: call `f.seek(0)` to go back to the beginning. This is a very common beginner bug:
>
> ```python
> with open("file.txt") as f:
>     content1 = f.read()    # reads everything
>     content2 = f.read()    # returns "" — pointer at EOF!
>     f.seek(0)              # reset pointer
>     content3 = f.read()    # reads everything again
> ```
>
> In practice, if you need the content multiple times, store it in a variable: `content = f.read()` — then use `content` multiple times without re-reading.

**Q6. How do you read a file in chunks? Why would you need to?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> Use `f.read(size)` which reads up to `size` bytes:
>
> ```python
> CHUNK_SIZE = 8192  # 8KB chunks
> with open("large_file.txt", "r") as f:
>     while True:
>         chunk = f.read(CHUNK_SIZE)
>         if not chunk:
>             break
>         process(chunk)
> ```
>
> Why: (1) **Memory efficiency** — 10GB file, 8KB chunks = constant ~8KB memory. (2) **Network streaming** — send file chunks over network. (3) **Hash computation** — compute MD5/SHA of huge files. (4) **Binary processing** — images, videos, encrypted files. I use chunk reading in file upload handlers, hash verification, and data pipeline ingestion. The chunk size is a performance knob — larger chunks = fewer reads = faster, but more memory.

**Q7. What is the `strip()`, `rstrip()`, `lstrip()` usage pattern when reading files?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> When reading lines, `readline()` and file iteration include the `\n` newline character. Common patterns:
>
> - `line.strip()` — removes BOTH leading and trailing whitespace (including `\n`)
> - `line.rstrip('\n')` — removes ONLY the trailing newline (preserves leading spaces)
> - `line.rstrip()` — removes all trailing whitespace
> - `line.rstrip('\r\n')` — removes Windows/Unix newlines
>   I use `line.rstrip('\n')` most often — it removes newlines but preserves intentional leading spaces (important for indented config files or code). Using `strip()` is simpler but can accidentally remove meaningful leading whitespace. In CSV processing, never use `strip()` on values — embedded whitespace might be meaningful.

sections.title: Reading & Writing Text Files — Scenario-Based Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
**S1. You need to read a configuration file that might have BOM (Byte Order Mark) at the beginning. How do you handle it?**

> **Answer:**
>
> ```python
> import os
>
> def read_config_robust(filepath):
>     """
>     Read config file handling:
>     - BOM (Byte Order Mark) in UTF-8/UTF-16 files
>     - Windows/Unix line endings
>     - Empty lines and comments
>     - Various encodings
>     """
>     # Try UTF-8 with BOM first (common in Windows-generated files)
>     encodings_to_try = ['utf-8-sig', 'utf-8', 'utf-16', 'latin-1']
>
>     content = None
>     used_encoding = None
>
>     for encoding in encodings_to_try:
>         try:
>             with open(filepath, 'r', encoding=encoding) as f:
>                 content = f.read()
>                 used_encoding = encoding
>                 break
>         except (UnicodeDecodeError, UnicodeError):
>             continue
>
>     if content is None:
>         raise ValueError(f"Cannot decode file with any known encoding: {filepath}")
>
>     print(f"📖 Read with encoding: {used_encoding}")
>
>     config = {}
>     for line_num, line in enumerate(content.splitlines(), 1):
>         line = line.strip()
>         if not line or line.startswith(('#', ';', '//')):
>             continue
>         if '=' in line:
>             key, _, value = line.partition('=')
>             config[key.strip()] = value.strip()
>         elif ':' in line:
>             key, _, value = line.partition(':')
>             config[key.strip()] = value.strip()
>
>     return config
>
> # Create file with BOM (common from Windows Notepad)
> with open("bom_config.txt", 'wb') as f:
>     bom = b'\xef\xbb\xbf'  # UTF-8 BOM
>     f.write(bom + b"# Config with BOM\nHOST=localhost\nPORT=8080\n")
>
> config = read_config_robust("bom_config.txt")
> print("Config:", config)
> # Without 'utf-8-sig', HOST key would be '\ufeffHOST' (BOM included!)
>
> os.remove("bom_config.txt")
> ```

**S2. You're building a report generator that writes formatted tables to text files.**

> **Answer:**
>
> ```python
> import os
> from datetime import datetime
>
> class ReportWriter:
>     """
>     Writes formatted reports to text files.
>     Real world: daily reports, audit logs, data exports.
>     """
>     def __init__(self, filepath, encoding='utf-8'):
>         self.filepath = filepath
>         self.encoding = encoding
>         self.lines    = []
>
>     def add_header(self, title, subtitle=None):
>         width = 60
>         self.lines.append("=" * width)
>         self.lines.append(title.center(width))
>         if subtitle:
>             self.lines.append(subtitle.center(width))
>         self.lines.append(f"Generated: {datetime.now().strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')}".center(width))
>         self.lines.append("=" * width)
>         self.lines.append("")
>
>     def add_table(self, headers, rows, col_widths=None):
>         if not col_widths:
>             col_widths = [max(len(str(h)), max((len(str(r[i])) for r in rows), default=0))
>                          for i, h in enumerate(headers)]
>
>         # Header row
>         header_str = " | ".join(f"{h:<{w}}" for h, w in zip(headers, col_widths))
>         separator  = "-+-".join("-" * w for w in col_widths)
>
>         self.lines.append(header_str)
>         self.lines.append(separator)
>
>         # Data rows
>         for row in rows:
>             row_str = " | ".join(f"{str(v):<{w}}" for v, w in zip(row, col_widths))
>             self.lines.append(row_str)
>
>         self.lines.append("")
>
>     def add_summary(self, stats):
>         self.lines.append("SUMMARY:")
>         self.lines.append("-" * 40)
>         for key, value in stats.items():
>             self.lines.append(f"  {key:<25}: {value}")
>         self.lines.append("")
>
>     def save(self):
>         with open(self.filepath, 'w', encoding=self.encoding) as f:
>             f.write('\n'.join(self.lines))
>             f.write('\n')
>         print(f"✅ Report saved: {self.filepath}")
>
> # Usage
> report = ReportWriter("sales_report.txt")
> report.add_header("MONTHLY SALES REPORT", "January 2024")
>
> headers = ["Product", "Units", "Revenue", "Growth"]
> rows = [
>     ["Python Course",  "1,234", "$61,700",  "+23%"],
>     ["Django Guide",   "892",   "$44,600",  "+15%"],
>     ["Data Science",   "2,105", "$105,250", "+41%"],
>     ["ML Bootcamp",    "456",   "$45,600",  "+8%"],
> ]
> report.add_table(headers, rows, col_widths=[15, 8, 12, 8])
>
> report.add_summary({
>     "Total Products": "4",
>     "Total Revenue":  "$257,150",
>     "Average Growth": "+21.75%",
>     "Best Performer": "Data Science",
> })
>
> report.save()
>
> with open("sales_report.txt") as f:
>     print(f.read())
>
> os.remove("sales_report.txt")
> ```

**S3. How do you efficiently count lines, words, and characters in a very large file?**

> **Answer:**
>
> ```python
> import os
> import time
>
> def count_file_stats(filepath, encoding='utf-8'):
>     """
>     Memory-efficient file statistics counter.
>     Reads line by line — works for 100GB files.
>     """
>     stats = {
>         'lines':      0,
>         'words':      0,
>         'characters': 0,
>         'empty_lines':0,
>         'longest_line': 0,
>         'shortest_line': float('inf'),
>         'file_size_bytes': os.path.getsize(filepath),
>     }
>
>     start = time.perf_counter()
>
>     with open(filepath, 'r', encoding=encoding) as f:
>         for line in f:   # memory efficient iteration
>             stripped = line.rstrip('\n')
>             line_len = len(stripped)
>
>             stats['lines']      += 1
>             stats['characters'] += len(line)
>             stats['words']      += len(stripped.split())
>
>             if not stripped.strip():
>                 stats['empty_lines'] += 1
>
>             if line_len > stats['longest_line']:
>                 stats['longest_line'] = line_len
>
>             if line_len < stats['shortest_line'] and stripped:
>                 stats['shortest_line'] = line_len
>
>     elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
>
>     if stats['shortest_line'] == float('inf'):
>         stats['shortest_line'] = 0
>
>     stats['processing_time'] = f"{elapsed:.3f}s"
>     stats['throughput_MB_s'] = f"{stats['file_size_bytes'] / (1024*1024*elapsed):.1f}"
>     stats['avg_line_length'] = round(stats['characters'] / max(stats['lines'],1), 1)
>
>     return stats
>
> # Create sample file
> with open("big_sample.txt", "w") as f:
>     for i in range(10000):
>         f.write(f"Line {i:05d}: This is sample content for testing file statistics.\n")
>         if i % 100 == 0:
>             f.write("\n")  # empty lines every 100
>
> stats = count_file_stats("big_sample.txt")
> print("FILE STATISTICS:")
> print("=" * 40)
> for key, value in stats.items():
>     print(f"  {key:<25}: {value:>15}")
>
> os.remove("big_sample.txt")
> ```

**S4. You need to write a file that should be readable by other applications (Excel, Notepad). What do you need to consider?**

> **Answer:**
>
> ```python
> import os
> import sys
>
> def write_cross_app_compatible(filepath, data_lines, target_app="universal"):
>     """
>     Write files compatible with various applications.
>
>     Applications and their requirements:
>     - Excel/Notepad (Windows): UTF-8 with BOM, CRLF line endings
>     - Unix tools (Linux/Mac): UTF-8 no BOM, LF line endings
>     - Universal (safest): UTF-8 with BOM, configurable endings
>     """
>     configs = {
>         "windows_notepad": {
>             "encoding": "utf-8-sig",  # UTF-8 with BOM
>             "newline":  "\r\n",        # Windows CRLF
>         },
>         "excel": {
>             "encoding": "utf-8-sig",  # Excel needs BOM for UTF-8
>             "newline":  "\r\n",
>         },
>         "unix": {
>             "encoding": "utf-8",       # No BOM
>             "newline":  "\n",          # Unix LF
>         },
>         "universal": {
>             "encoding": "utf-8-sig",
>             "newline":  os.linesep,    # Use OS native
>         },
>     }
>
>     cfg = configs.get(target_app, configs["universal"])
>
>     # Write with explicit newline control
>     with open(filepath, 'w',
>               encoding=cfg["encoding"],
>               newline='') as f:   # newline='' means we control newlines ourselves
>         for line in data_lines:
>             f.write(line + cfg["newline"])
>
>     # Verify what was written
>     with open(filepath, 'rb') as f:
>         first_bytes = f.read(10)
>
>     has_bom = first_bytes.startswith(b'\xef\xbb\xbf')
>     print(f"File: {filepath}")
>     print(f"  Encoding  : {cfg['encoding']}")
>     print(f"  Has BOM   : {has_bom}")
>     print(f"  First bytes: {first_bytes.hex()}")
>
> lines = ["Report Title", "=" * 20, "Item 1: $100", "Item 2: $200", "Total: $300"]
>
> write_cross_app_compatible("for_excel.txt",    lines, "excel")
> write_cross_app_compatible("for_unix.txt",     lines, "unix")
> write_cross_app_compatible("universal.txt",    lines, "universal")
>
> for f in ["for_excel.txt", "for_unix.txt", "universal.txt"]:
>     os.remove(f)
> ```

**S5. How do you implement a simple template file system using Python file reading?**

> **Answer:**
>
> ```python
> import os
> import re
> from datetime import datetime
>
> class FileTemplateEngine:
>     """
>     Simple template file reader and renderer.
>     Real world: email templates, report templates, HTML generation.
>     Template syntax: {{variable_name}} and {{variable_name|default_value}}
>     """
>     def __init__(self, template_dir="templates"):
>         self.template_dir = template_dir
>         os.makedirs(template_dir, exist_ok=True)
>
>     def load_template(self, template_name):
>         """Read template file"""
>         path = os.path.join(self.template_dir, template_name)
>         if not os.path.exists(path):
>             raise FileNotFoundError(f"Template not found: {path}")
>         with open(path, 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f:
>             return f.read()
>
>     def render(self, template_name, context):
>         """Render template with context variables"""
>         template = self.load_template(template_name)
>
>         def replace_var(match):
>             var_part = match.group(1)
>             if '|' in var_part:
>                 var_name, default = var_part.split('|', 1)
>             else:
>                 var_name, default = var_part, ''
>
>             var_name = var_name.strip()
>             value    = context.get(var_name, default.strip())
>             return str(value)
>
>         rendered = re.sub(r'\{\{(.*?)\}\}', replace_var, template)
>         return rendered
>
>     def render_to_file(self, template_name, context, output_path):
>         """Render and save to file"""
>         content = self.render(template_name, context)
>         with open(output_path, 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
>             f.write(content)
>         return output_path
>
> # Setup
> engine = FileTemplateEngine("templates")
>
> # Create templates
> with open("templates/email.txt", "w") as f:
>     f.write("""Dear {{first_name}} {{last_name|User}},
>
> Thank you for your order #{{order_id}}.
>
> Order Details:
>   Product : {{product_name|Unknown Product}}
>   Amount  : ${{amount}}
>   Status  : {{status|Pending}}
>   Date    : {{date}}
>
> Best regards,
> {{company_name|Our Company}} Support Team
> """)
>
> # Render template
> context = {
>     "first_name":    "John",
>     "last_name":     "Doe",
>     "order_id":      "ORD-2024-001",
>     "product_name":  "Python Masterclass",
>     "amount":        "99.99",
>     "status":        "Confirmed",
>     "date":          datetime.now().strftime("%B %d, %Y"),
>     "company_name":  "PyLearn Academy",
> }
>
> result = engine.render("email.txt", context)
> print(result)
>
> # Cleanup
> import shutil
> shutil.rmtree("templates", ignore_errors=True)
> ```

**S6. You need to read a file and process only lines matching certain patterns. Build an efficient filter.**

> **Answer:**
>
> ```python
> import os
> import re
> from typing import Iterator, Callable
>
> class FileLineFilter:
>     """
>     Efficient line-by-line file filter.
>     Real world: log analysis, data extraction, report generation.
>     Generator-based — memory efficient for huge files.
>     """
>     def __init__(self, filepath, encoding='utf-8'):
>         self.filepath = filepath
>         self.encoding = encoding
>
>     def filtered_lines(self, *filters) -> Iterator[tuple]:
>         """
>         Generator: yields (line_num, line) for lines passing ALL filters.
>         filters: callables taking a string, returning bool
>         """
>         with open(self.filepath, 'r', encoding=self.encoding) as f:
>             for line_num, line in enumerate(f, 1):
>                 line_stripped = line.rstrip('\n')
>                 if all(f(line_stripped) for f in filters):
>                     yield line_num, line_stripped
>
>     def grep(self, pattern, ignore_case=False) -> Iterator[tuple]:
>         """Find lines matching regex pattern"""
>         flags = re.IGNORECASE if ignore_case else 0
>         regex = re.compile(pattern, flags)
>         return self.filtered_lines(lambda l: bool(regex.search(l)))
>
>     def between_markers(self, start_marker, end_marker) -> Iterator[str]:
>         """Extract lines between two markers"""
>         inside  = False
>         with open(self.filepath, 'r', encoding=self.encoding) as f:
>             for line in f:
>                 if start_marker in line:
>                     inside = True
>                     continue
>                 if end_marker in line:
>                     inside = False
>                     continue
>                 if inside:
>                     yield line.rstrip('\n')
>
>     def extract_fields(self, pattern, group_names=None):
>         """Extract regex groups from matching lines"""
>         regex = re.compile(pattern)
>         with open(self.filepath, 'r', encoding=self.encoding) as f:
>             for line_num, line in enumerate(f, 1):
>                 match = regex.search(line)
>                 if match:
>                     if group_names:
>                         yield {name: match.group(name) for name in group_names}
>                     else:
>                         yield match.groups()
>
> # Create sample log file
> with open("app.log", "w") as f:
>     logs = [
>         "2024-01-15 10:00:01 INFO  [auth] User alice logged in from 192.168.1.100",
>         "2024-01-15 10:00:05 ERROR [db]   Connection timeout after 30s",
>         "2024-01-15 10:00:10 INFO  [api]  GET /users returned 200",
>         "2024-01-15 10:00:15 ERROR [api]  POST /orders returned 500: DB error",
>         "2024-01-15 10:00:20 WARN  [auth] Failed login for user bob (3rd attempt)",
>         "2024-01-15 10:00:25 INFO  [db]   Connection restored",
>         "2024-01-15 10:00:30 ERROR [auth] Account locked: user bob",
>     ]
>     f.write('\n'.join(logs))
>
> fltr = FileLineFilter("app.log")
>
> print("=== ERROR Lines ===")
> for num, line in fltr.grep("ERROR"):
>     print(f"  L{num}: {line}")
>
> print("\n=== Auth Module Lines ===")
> for num, line in fltr.grep(r"\[auth\]"):
>     print(f"  L{num}: {line}")
>
> print("\n=== Extract IP Addresses ===")
> ip_pattern = r"(?P<timestamp>\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2} \d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2}) (?P<level>\w+).*?(?P<ip>\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+)"
> for fields in fltr.extract_fields(ip_pattern, ["timestamp","level","ip"]):
>     print(f"  {fields}")
>
> os.remove("app.log")
> ```

**S7. How do you implement a file-based task queue where tasks persist across program restarts?**

> **Answer:**
>
> ```python
> import os
> import json
> from datetime import datetime
>
> class PersistentTaskQueue:
>     """
>     File-based task queue that survives program restarts.
>     Each task stored as a JSON line (JSONL format).
>     Real world: job queues, retry systems, audit trails.
>     """
>     def __init__(self, queue_file="task_queue.jsonl"):
>         self.queue_file = queue_file
>         self.processed_file = queue_file.replace('.jsonl', '_processed.jsonl')
>
>     def enqueue(self, task_type, payload, priority=5):
>         """Add task to queue (append to file)"""
>         task = {
>             "id":        f"TASK_{datetime.now().strftime('%Y%m%d_%H%M%S_%f')}",
>             "type":      task_type,
>             "payload":   payload,
>             "priority":  priority,
>             "status":    "pending",
>             "created_at":datetime.now().isoformat(),
>             "attempts":  0,
>         }
>         # Append mode — safe to call from multiple places
>         with open(self.queue_file, 'a', encoding='utf-8') as f:
>             f.write(json.dumps(task) + '\n')  # JSONL format
>
>         print(f"✅ Enqueued: {task['id']} ({task_type})")
>         return task['id']
>
>     def get_pending(self):
>         """Read all pending tasks"""
>         if not os.path.exists(self.queue_file):
>             return []
>         tasks = []
>         with open(self.queue_file, 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f:
>             for line in f:
>                 line = line.strip()
>                 if not line:
>                     continue
>                 try:
>                     task = json.loads(line)
>                     if task.get('status') == 'pending':
>                         tasks.append(task)
>                 except json.JSONDecodeError:
>                     continue
>         # Sort by priority (lower = higher priority) then by created time
>         return sorted(tasks, key=lambda t: (t['priority'], t['created_at']))
>
>     def mark_complete(self, task_id):
>         """Mark task as complete — rewrite file without completed task"""
>         self._update_task_status(task_id, 'completed')
>
>     def mark_failed(self, task_id, error_msg):
>         """Mark task as failed with error message"""
>         self._update_task_status(task_id, 'failed', {"error": error_msg})
>
>     def _update_task_status(self, task_id, new_status, extra=None):
>         """Update a specific task's status by rewriting the file"""
>         if not os.path.exists(self.queue_file):
>             return
>
>         updated_lines = []
>         with open(self.queue_file, 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f:
>             for line in f:
>                 line = line.strip()
>                 if not line:
>                     continue
>                 try:
>                     task = json.loads(line)
>                     if task.get('id') == task_id:
>                         task['status'] = new_status
>                         task['updated_at'] = datetime.now().isoformat()
>                         task['attempts'] = task.get('attempts', 0) + 1
>                         if extra:
>                             task.update(extra)
>                     updated_lines.append(json.dumps(task))
>                 except json.JSONDecodeError:
>                     updated_lines.append(line)
>
>         # Atomic write
>         with open(self.queue_file + '.tmp', 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
>             f.write('\n'.join(updated_lines) + '\n')
>         os.replace(self.queue_file + '.tmp', self.queue_file)
>
>     def process_next(self, processor_func):
>         """Process next pending task"""
>         pending = self.get_pending()
>         if not pending:
>             print("📭 No pending tasks")
>             return None
>
>         task = pending[0]
>         print(f"🔄 Processing: {task['id']} ({task['type']})")
>
>         try:
>             result = processor_func(task)
>             self.mark_complete(task['id'])
>             print(f"✅ Completed: {task['id']}")
>             return result
>         except Exception as e:
>             self.mark_failed(task['id'], str(e))
>             print(f"❌ Failed: {task['id']} — {e}")
>             return None
>
> # Demo
> queue = PersistentTaskQueue("demo_queue.jsonl")
>
> # Add tasks
> queue.enqueue("send_email", {"to": "user@example.com", "subject": "Welcome"}, priority=1)
> queue.enqueue("generate_report", {"type": "monthly", "month": "2024-01"}, priority=3)
> queue.enqueue("resize_image", {"path": "/uploads/photo.jpg", "size": "800x600"}, priority=5)
>
> print(f"\nPending tasks: {len(queue.get_pending())}")
>
> # Process tasks
> def dummy_processor(task):
>     print(f"  → Processing {task['type']} with payload {task['payload']}")
>     return "done"
>
> queue.process_next(dummy_processor)
> queue.process_next(dummy_processor)
>
> print(f"\nRemaining pending: {len(queue.get_pending())}")
>
> # Cleanup
> for f in ["demo_queue.jsonl", "demo_queue.jsonl.tmp"]:
>     if os.path.exists(f):
>         os.remove(f)
> ```

sections.title: OS Module — Complete Guide — Conceptual Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
**Q1. What is the difference between `os.mkdir()` and `os.makedirs()`?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `os.mkdir("a/b/c")` creates **only ONE directory** — if `a/b` doesn't exist, it raises `FileNotFoundError`. `os.makedirs("a/b/c")` creates the **entire path** including all intermediate directories (like `mkdir -p`). The `exist_ok=True` parameter prevents `FileExistsError` if the directory already exists. In production, I always use `os.makedirs(path, exist_ok=True)` — it's idempotent (safe to call multiple times). `os.mkdir()` is only useful when you know the parent exists and want to fail if the directory already exists. Real bug: `os.mkdir("logs")` fails in production if `logs/` already exists from a previous run — `makedirs` with `exist_ok=True` prevents this.

**Q2. What is the difference between `os.remove()`, `os.rmdir()`, and `shutil.rmtree()`?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `os.remove()` deletes **a single file** only — raises `IsADirectoryError` on directories. `os.rmdir()` deletes **an empty directory** — raises `OSError` if directory has content. `shutil.rmtree()` deletes a **directory and ALL its contents** recursively (like `rm -rf`). In production, `shutil.rmtree()` is dangerous — always add a safety check:
>
> ```python
> def safe_rmtree(path, must_contain="expected_subdir"):
>     """Safety check before deleting tree"""
>     if not os.path.exists(path):
>         return
>     if must_contain and not os.path.exists(os.path.join(path, must_contain)):
>         raise ValueError(f"Safety check failed: {path} doesn't contain {must_contain}")
>     shutil.rmtree(path)
> ```
>
> I've seen a bug where `shutil.rmtree(base_path)` was called with `base_path = "/"` due to a variable assignment error — deleted the entire filesystem!

**Q3. What does `os.walk()` return and how do you use it?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `os.walk(top)` is a generator that yields `(dirpath, dirnames, filenames)` tuples for every directory in the tree. `dirpath` is the path to the current directory; `dirnames` is a list of subdirectory names; `filenames` is a list of file names in that directory. Crucial trick: you can modify `dirnames` in-place to skip certain directories:
>
> ```python
> for root, dirs, files in os.walk("."):
>     dirs[:] = [d for d in dirs
>                if d not in {'.git', '__pycache__', 'node_modules', '.venv'}]
>     for filename in files:
>         filepath = os.path.join(root, filename)
>         # process filepath
> ```
>
> I use `os.walk()` for: finding all files of a type, calculating directory sizes, building file indexes, implementing search tools.

**Q4. What is the difference between `os.rename()` and `shutil.move()`?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `os.rename()` works only on the **same filesystem** — it's an atomic operation (just changes directory entry). If source and destination are on different filesystems, it raises `OSError`. `shutil.move()` works **across filesystems** — it copies the file then deletes the source. In practice: for simple renaming within same directory, `os.rename()` is atomic and faster. For moving between drives or network locations, use `shutil.move()`. Also: `os.replace()` is like `os.rename()` but atomically replaces the destination if it exists — use for atomic file updates. I use `os.replace()` for config file updates to prevent partial-write corruption.

**Q5. How do you get file metadata with `os.stat()`?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `os.stat(path)` returns a `stat_result` object with file metadata:
>
> ```python
> stat = os.stat("file.txt")
> stat.st_size   # file size in bytes
> stat.st_mtime  # last modification time (Unix timestamp)
> stat.st_atime  # last access time
> stat.st_ctime  # creation time (Windows) or metadata change (Unix!)
> stat.st_mode   # file permissions (use stat module to interpret)
> stat.st_uid    # user ID of owner (Unix)
> stat.st_gid    # group ID of owner (Unix)
> ```
>
> Key gotcha: `st_ctime` is NOT creation time on Linux/Mac — it's metadata change time (last chmod, chown, rename). On Windows it IS creation time. For actual modification time, always use `st_mtime`. In my monitoring tools, I use `st_mtime` to detect changed files and `st_size` for zero-byte file detection.

**Q6. What is `os.path.join()` and why should you always use it instead of string concatenation?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `os.path.join()` constructs file paths correctly for the current OS, handling path separators automatically. String concatenation `"/path/" + "file.txt"` works but is fragile: (1) You might forget the separator, (2) You might double it (`/path//file`), (3) On Windows it should be `\`, not `/`. `os.path.join("home", "user", "file.txt")` → `home/user/file.txt` (Unix) or `home\user\file.txt` (Windows). Even better: use `pathlib.Path` (Python 3.6+) with the `/` operator: `Path("home") / "user" / "file.txt"`. I never concatenate paths with `+` — it's a code smell in any code review I do.

**Q7. What is the difference between `os.path` and `pathlib.Path`?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `os.path` is the **traditional function-based** approach (collection of functions). `pathlib.Path` is the **modern object-oriented** approach (Python 3.4+). `pathlib` is preferred for new code:
>
> ```python
> # os.path (old)
> import os.path
> path = os.path.join("home", "user", "file.txt")
> if os.path.exists(path) and os.path.isfile(path):
>     size = os.path.getsize(path)
>     name = os.path.basename(path)
>
> # pathlib (modern, better)
> from pathlib import Path
> p = Path("home") / "user" / "file.txt"
> if p.exists() and p.is_file():
>     size = p.stat().st_size
>     name = p.name
>     stem = p.stem      # filename without extension
>     suffix = p.suffix  # just the extension
> ```
>
> `pathlib` advantages: more readable, chainable, has methods like `.read_text()`, `.write_text()`, `.glob()`, `.rglob()`. I refactor all `os.path` code to `pathlib` in new projects.

quiz.question: What is the difference between open() with close() vs using with statement?
options: 5-Year Exp Answer: > The encoding parameter tells Python how to convert bytes (what's stored on disk) to characters (what you see in Python strings).
5-Year Exp Answer: > RotatingFileHandler automatically rotates log files when they reach a size limit, keeping N backup files: > > > > Without rotation: a long-running…
5-Year Exp Answer: > os.path is the traditional function-based approach (collection of functions). pathlib.Path is the modern object-oriented approach (Python 3.4+).…
5-Year Exp Answer: > Both open files, but the with statement (context manager) is vastly superior.
quiz.explanation: 5-Year Exp Answer: Both open files, but the with statement (context manager) is vastly superior. With close(): if an exception occurs between open() and close(), the file is NEVER closed — causing file descriptor leaks. With the with statement, Python guarantees the file is closed via __exit__() method even if an exception occurs.

5-Year Exp Answer: > Python (and the OS) use write buffers for performance — data isn't written to disk immediately but accumulated in memory first.

quiz.explanation: 5-Year Exp Answer: There are 8 core modes: 'r' (read-only, default), 'w' (write, creates/overwrites), 'a' (append, preserves content), 'x' (exclusive create, fails if exists). Then combinations: 'r+' (read+write without truncating), 'w+' (write+read with truncating), 'a+' (append+read). Add 'b' for binary: 'rb', 'wb', 'ab'.

quiz.question: What does the encoding parameter do and why is UTF-8 the standard?
options: 5-Year Exp Answer: > os.path.join() constructs file paths correctly for the current OS, handling path separators automatically.
5-Year Exp Answer: > > > > JSONDecodeError subclasses ValueError.
5-Year Exp Answer: > json.load(f) reads from a file object — the file must be opened first. json.loads(s) parses a string (the 's' stands for string).
5-Year Exp Answer: > The encoding parameter tells Python how to convert bytes (what's stored on disk) to characters (what you see in Python strings).
quiz.explanation: 5-Year Exp Answer: The encoding parameter tells Python how to convert bytes (what's stored on disk) to characters (what you see in Python strings). If you open a UTF-8 file with ASCII encoding, you get UnicodeDecodeError for any non-ASCII character. UTF-8 is the web standard — it can represent every Unicode character while being backward compatible with ASCII.

quiz.question: What is the difference between text mode and binary mode?

quiz.explanation: 5-Year Exp Answer: Text mode ('r', 'w'): Python automatically handles encoding/decoding and newline translation (\n on Unix, \r\n on Windows). You work with str objects. Binary mode ('rb', 'wb'): no encoding/decoding, no newline translation.

quiz.question: What happens to the write buffer when a file is closed?
options: 5-Year Exp Answer: > os.mkdir("a/b/c") creates only ONE directory — if a/b doesn't exist, it raises FileNotFoundError. os.makedirs("a/b/c") creates the entire path…
5-Year Exp Answer: > There are 8 core modes: 'r' (read-only, default), 'w' (write, creates/overwrites), 'a' (append, preserves content), 'x' (exclusive create, fails if…
5-Year Exp Answer: > All file exceptions inherit from OSError (also aliased as IOError for backwards compatibility).
5-Year Exp Answer: > Python (and the OS) use write buffers for performance — data isn't written to disk immediately but accumulated in memory first.
quiz.explanation: 5-Year Exp Answer: Python (and the OS) use write buffers for performance — data isn't written to disk immediately but accumulated in memory first. When you call close() (or exit the with block), Python flushes the buffer — forces all buffered data to disk. If your program crashes before closing, buffered data is LOST.
